diagnosis: Verification bias in a diagnostic-accuracy study
mechanism: Verification bias occurs when receipt of the reference-standard test depends on the index-test result or related clinical suspicion, so disease status is not verified comparably across index-test groups and calculated diagnostic accuracy becomes biased.
vignette: Researchers evaluate a new noninvasive test for pancreatic cancer. Every patient with a positive index test undergoes biopsy, but patients with a negative index test undergo biopsy only if the treating physician remains highly suspicious for cancer. Sensitivity and specificity are calculated only among patients who underwent biopsy.
lead: Which of the following biases is introduced by this study design?
distractor_notes: Lead-time bias concerns apparent survival gains caused by earlier diagnosis without delayed death; it is not a reference-standard ascertainment problem.
Length-time bias results when screening preferentially detects slower-growing disease; it does not describe selective biopsy based on the index-test result.
Recall bias arises from differential accuracy of remembered past exposures and is unrelated to selective use of a diagnostic reference standard.
Immortal time bias arises from misclassified follow-up during which an outcome cannot occur in a later-defined exposure group; it is not the defect in this diagnostic-accuracy study.
key_expl: A diagnostic-accuracy study ideally verifies true disease status with the reference standard independent of the index-test result. If positive tests are much more likely than negative tests to receive the reference standard, restricting analysis to verified patients distorts the apparent sensitivity and specificity. This is verification, or workup, bias.
objective: Recognize verification bias when the probability of receiving the diagnostic reference standard depends on the index-test result or clinical suspicion.
